gloss: be brought low, humble oneself, be subdued; subdue; Canaan, Canaanite, trader
summary: To be brought low and to bring low. The niphal is to be subdued, of a nation that no longer lifts its head (Jdg 8:28), and above all to humble oneself before Yahweh, as Ahab, Hezekiah, Manasseh and Josiah did and were heard (1Ki 21:29; 2Ch 7:14; 33:12; 34:27); the hiphil is Yahweh, or the king he empowers, subduing enemies and bringing the proud low (Deu 9:3; Job 40:12). The same letters spell כְּנַעַן, Canaan, son of Ham and the land promised to Abraham and his seed, its people the כְּנַעֲנִי, and, from the Phoenician traders of the coast, “merchant”. Scripture never explains the name, but Noah's curse makes Canaan “a servant of servants” (Gen 9:25), and the verb is used of God subduing the king of Canaan and the Canaanites before Israel (Jdg 4:23; Neh 9:24).

words.gloss: be subdued, humble oneself; subdue, humble
words.summary: Thirty-six times, only in the niphal and hiphil. Its opposites are lifting the head (Jdg 8:28) and the pride of the heart (2Ch 32:26; Job 40:11–12); its parallel is הִשְׁפִּיל “bring low” (Job 40:11–12). Where a man is the subject of the niphal it is nearly always before Yahweh, and Yahweh's answer follows.

senses.definition: Of a nation beaten in war: to be brought under another's hand, so that it no longer lifts its head or comes into the land.

evidence.note: “וַיִּכָּנַע Midian before the sons of Israel, and they did not again lift their head”: the opposite of lifting the head.
“Moab וַתִּכָּנַע that day under the hand of Israel, and the land had rest eighty years.”
“The Philistines were subdued, and did not again come into the border of Israel.”
The sons of Ammon subdued before Israel.
The Philistines at Gezer.
“The sons of Israel were subdued at that time, and the sons of Judah prevailed, because they leaned on Yahweh.”
“Their enemies oppressed them, וַיִּכָּנְעוּ under their hand.”

senses.definition: To lower oneself before Yahweh: to give up pride and own one's sin, with prayer, mourning or tearing of clothes. Yahweh sees it and turns or delays his wrath; refusing to do it brings the judgment on.

evidence.note: “If then their uncircumcised heart יִכָּנַע and they accept the punishment of their iniquity”: the turning that brings the covenant to remembrance (v. 42).
“Do you see how Ahab נִכְנַע before me? Because he has humbled himself before me, I will not bring the evil in his days”: after he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth and fasted (v. 27).
Josiah: “because your heart was tender, וַתִּכָּנַע before Yahweh … and tore your clothes and wept before me, I also have heard you.”
“If my people … יִכָּנְעוּ and pray and seek my face and turn from their evil ways, then I will hear from heaven and forgive their sin and heal their land.”
The princes and Rehoboam humbled themselves and said “Yahweh is righteous”; Yahweh saw that they humbled themselves and granted some deliverance.
Men of Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem for the passover, when others mocked.
“Hezekiah וַיִּכָּנַע for the pride (בְּגֹבַהּ) of his heart”: humbling is the opposite of a lifted heart.
Manasseh in distress “entreated Yahweh his God, and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers”, and Yahweh heard him and brought him back (v. 13).
Amon “did not humble himself before Yahweh, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself.”
Zedekiah “did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet speaking from the mouth of Yahweh.”

senses.definition: To bring a nation or enemy under, by war: done by Yahweh before Israel, or by David as Yahweh promised.

evidence.note: “He will destroy them and he יַכְנִיעֵם before you, and you shall drive them out”: of the nations of the land.
“God וַיַּכְנַע on that day Jabin king of Canaan before the sons of Israel.”
“The sons went in and possessed the land, וַתַּכְנַע before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gave them into their hands.”
“David struck the Philistines וַיַּכְנִיעֵם”; also 1Ch 18:1.
Yahweh to David: “I will subdue all your enemies, and … Yahweh will build you a house.”
“Soon I would subdue their enemies” if Israel would walk in his ways (v. 14).
“You subdue the uproar of strangers, as heat by the shade of a cloud.”

senses.definition: To bring down the proud, or one's own people for their sin, so that they stumble and are without help.

evidence.note: “Look on every proud one הַכְנִיעֵהוּ, and tread down the wicked where they stand”, after “look on every proud one and bring him low (וְהַשְׁפִּילֵהוּ)” (v. 11).
“He brought down (וַיַּכְנַע) their heart with labour; they stumbled and there was no helper.”
“Yahweh brought Judah low because of Ahaz.”

greek.gloss: make low, humble; (passive, middle) humble oneself

evidence.note: “Humble yourselves (ταπεινώθητε) before the Lord, and he will lift you up”: the humbling of 2Ch 7:14 and 33:12, and Yahweh's answer.
“Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, that he may lift you up in due time.”
“Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.”

parallels.note: The hiphil “bring low”, in the next line of the same charge to bring down the proud.

opposites.note: Lifting the head: what a subdued nation no longer does.
Pride of heart, which Hezekiah humbled himself for.

phrases.gloss: be subdued under the hand of

words.gloss: Canaan: son of Ham; his land and people; (in trade) merchants
words.summary: About ninety times. It names a man, his land and his people, as the names of nations do in Gen 10, and because the Canaanites of the coast (Tyre and Sidon) were traders it also means merchant, merchants. The neighbours' own records spell the same name (Phoenician knʿn, Egyptian Knꜥn, Akkadian Kinaḫnum). How the name comes from the root's sense “be brought low” scripture does not say; it is set beside it in Noah's curse (Gen 9:25) and in the verb's use for subduing Canaan's king and people (Jdg 4:23; Neh 9:24), which rests on little. The corpus files every token under the merchant key k.cd.ad as well.

senses.definition: The fourth son of Ham, father of Sidon, Heth and the peoples of the land, whom Noah cursed to be a servant of servants to his brothers.

evidence.note: “Ham was the father of Canaan.”
“Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be to his brothers”; again vv. 26–27.
Canaan fathered Sidon, Heth, the Jebusite, the Amorite … “and afterward the clans of the Canaanite spread abroad.”

senses.definition: The land west of the Jordan, from Sidon to Gaza, where Abraham sojourned and which Yahweh promised to him and his seed for an everlasting possession; Israel's land.

evidence.note: “The border of the Canaanite was from Sidon … to Gaza … to Sodom and Gomorrah.”
Terah set out from Ur “to go into the land of Canaan”.
“I will give to you and to your seed after you the land of your sojournings, all the land of Canaan, for an everlasting possession.”
Sarah buried in Machpelah “in the land of Canaan”.
The famine in Egypt and Canaan, of which Act 7:11 speaks.
“To give you the land of Canaan, to be your God.”
“The land that falls to you for an inheritance, the land of Canaan by its borders”, traced in vv. 3–12.
The covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: “To you I will give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance”; also 1Ch 16:18.
Israel “sacrificed to the idols of Canaan, and the land was polluted with blood”.

senses.gloss: Canaan, its people; the Phoenician coast
senses.definition: The land's inhabitants as a whole, and in the prophets the trading cities of the coast, Tyre and Sidon; its language is the Hebrew of Israel's neighbours.

evidence.note: “All the inhabitants of Canaan melted away.”
“The kings of Canaan fought at Taanach.”
In the burden of Tyre: “Yahweh has commanded concerning Canaan, to destroy its strongholds.”
Five cities in Egypt “speaking the language of Canaan and swearing to Yahweh of Armies”.

senses.definition: A trader, or traders as a class, named after the Canaanite merchants of the coast: weighers of silver, a city of merchants, a man with false scales.

evidence.note: “He brought it to a land of כְּנַעַן, he set it in a city of merchants (רֹכְלִים)”: Babylon, so not the land of Canaan.
“All the people of כְּנַעַן are undone; all who weigh out silver are cut off.”
“כְּנַעַן, in his hand are false scales; he loves to oppress”: Ephraim the dishonest trader.
“To the land of כְּנַעַן, Chaldea”: Babylon as a land of trade, as Ezk 17:4.

evidence.locator: Χαναάν renders כְּנַעַן ×81 (Gen.11.31; 17.8; 47.13 …); Φοινίκη at Exo.16.35

evidence.note: “A famine came over all the land of Egypt and Canaan”: Gen 41:54; 47:13.
“Having destroyed seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance.”

words.summary: The gentilic of כְּנַעַן (feminine כְּנַעֲנִית), usually with the article as a collective, “the Canaanite”: first in the lists of the peoples of the land, and like כְּנַעַן also “trader”. The corpus files every token under the trader key k.cd.af as well.

senses.definition: The people of the land before Israel, named with the Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Hivite and Jebusite as the nations Yahweh would drive out; a man or woman of that people.

evidence.note: “The Canaanite was then in the land”, where Yahweh promised it to Abraham's seed (v. 7).
Last but one in the list of the land's peoples given to Abraham's seed (vv. 18–21).
“You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanite.”
Judah married the daughter of a Canaanite man, Shua; also 1Ch 2:3.
“Shaul the son of the Canaanite woman (הַכְּנַעֲנִית).”
“To the place of the Canaanite and the Hittite and the Amorite … a land flowing with milk and honey.”
Seven nations greater and mightier than Israel, the Canaanite among them, to be cleared away.
“The Canaanite, the king of Arad, who dwelt in the Negev.”
“When the sons of Israel grew strong they put the Canaanite to forced labour, but did not drive them out”: the servitude of Gen 9:25.
Israel dwelt among the Canaanites and took their daughters.
To Jerusalem: “your origin and your birth are of the land of the Canaanite.”
“You made the covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanite … to his seed.”

senses.definition: A trader, buying and selling goods: the Canaanite as the merchant of the land.

evidence.note: “She makes linen garments and sells them, and delivers belts to the כְּנַעֲנִי”: the one who buys to sell.
“Will they divide him among כְּנַעֲנִים?”, after “will companions bargain over him?”
Tyre, “whose merchants (סֹחֲרֶיהָ) are princes, whose כִּנְעָנֶיהָ are the honoured of the earth.”

“There shall no longer be a כְּנַעֲנִי in the house of Yahweh of Armies in that day”: a trader, or a Canaanite; Jesus drove the traders out, “do not make my Father's house a house of trade” (Jhn 2:16).
“Do not make my Father's house a house of trade (ἐμπορίου).”

evidence.locator: Χανααναῖος renders כְּנַעֲנִי ×57 (Gen.12.6; Exo.3.8; Deu.7.1 …); Zec.14.21 → Χανααναῖος

evidence.note: “A Canaanite woman (γυνὴ Χαναναία) from those regions”, of Tyre and Sidon (v. 21).

words.summary: Once, of the belongings gathered up for exile. How it comes from the root is not clear: it may be what is pressed together into a pack (compare the Aramaic “press”), or a trader's wares (from כְּנַעַן “merchant”); nothing in scripture fixes either, and no cognate yet shares its meaning, so its tie to the root rests on little.

senses.definition: What a besieged dweller gathers up from the ground to carry away into exile.

evidence.note: “Gather up your כִּנְעָה from the land, you who dwell under siege”, for “I am slinging out the inhabitants of the land” (v. 18).

words.summary: The Peshitta's Canaan (ܟܢܥܢ), where the Greek has Χαναάν. SEDRA files it under its own root with the gentilic, and no Syriac verb of the root.

senses.definition: The land of the fathers, given to Israel.

evidence.note: “A famine came on all Egypt and on the land of ܟܢܥܢ.”
Seven nations destroyed “in the land of ܟܢܥܢ”.

words.summary: The Peshitta's gentilic (ܟܢܥܢܝܐ, feminine ܟܢܥܢܝܬܐ), where the Greek has Χαναναῖος.

senses.definition: A woman of the region of Tyre and Sidon, of the old people of the land.

evidence.note: “A ܟܢܥܢܝܬܐ woman from those borders”, of Tyre and Sidon (v. 21); Mark calls her a Syrophoenician (Mrk 7:26).

cognates.gloss: press, oppress; (passive participle) depressed, mournful; (ithpeel, ithpaal) lower oneself, be humble; bow to a superior
cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic, in the Targums and Talmud. The Targum of 1Ki 21:29 uses the reflexive for Ahab's humbling, and the Jerusalem Talmud's מִתְכַּנְּעִין is to humble oneself in penitence: the same sense as the Hebrew niphal. Jewish Aramaic does not keep ʿ and ġ apart, so it shows no sound behind ע.

evidence.locator: K00866, s.v. כְּנַע (ch.), citing Y. Ter. XI, 48b (part. pass. כְּנִיעִין, low-spirited); Targ. Y. Gen. XVI, 9; Targ. I Kings XXI, 29; Y. Taan. III, 66c (מִתְכַּנְּעִין, humble themselves in penitence); M. Kat. 16b (bow to)

cognates.note: The name in the speech of the coastal Canaanites themselves, the traders of Tyre and Sidon whom the prophets call כְּנַעַן (Isa 23:11).
The land's name in cuneiform. Akkadian has no ʿ, and its ḫ here stands for the West Semitic guttural; it cannot show whether that was ʿ or ġ.

evidence.locator: Akkadian Kinaḫnum, name: Canaan; 𒆳𒆠𒈾𒄴𒈾 (ᵏᵘʳki-na-aḫ-na), cuneiform form of Kinaḫnum

cognates.note: The Semitic name taken into Egyptian, written with ꜥ. Egyptian writes the other sound, ġ, with g, as in Gaza gꜣḏꜣty for עַזָּה, so the ꜥ here points to ʿ behind the name's ע.

evidence.locator: tla854886, Knꜥn “Kanaan” (Ahituv, Canaanite Toponyms, 83 ff.); tla854885, Pꜣ-Knꜥn
Egyptian gꜣḏꜣty, name: Gaza, compare Hebrew עַזָּה

doctrine.statement: Every time a king humbles himself (נִכְנַע) before Yahweh, Yahweh is said to see or hear it and to hold back his wrath: Ahab after Naboth's blood (1Ki 21:27–29), Rehoboam and his princes (2Ch 12:6–7, 12), Hezekiah after the pride of his heart (2Ch 32:26), Manasseh after all his idols, who was heard and brought back to Jerusalem (2Ch 33:12–13), and Josiah (2Ki 22:19). Amon and Zedekiah would not humble themselves, and judgment came (2Ch 33:23; 36:12). Yahweh's promise to Solomon makes it the condition of forgiveness: “if my people humble themselves and pray and seek my face and turn from their evil ways, then I will hear … and forgive” (2Ch 7:14), and the law had said the same of the scattered nation (Lev 26:41–42). The apostles repeat it: “humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will lift you up” (Jas 4:10; 1Pe 5:6). From the verses: the way back to God for a sinner, however great his sin, is to lower himself before God, own his sin and turn; God does not refuse it.

Yahweh promised Abraham: “I will give to you and to your seed after you … all the land of Canaan for an everlasting possession” (Gen 17:8), and confirmed it to Isaac and Jacob (Psa 105:9–11). Abraham himself lived in it only as a stranger, buying a grave (Gen 23:4, 19); Stephen says God “gave him no inheritance in it, not even a foot's breadth, yet promised to give it to him for a possession, and to his seed after him” (Act 7:5), and Hebrews says he and Isaac and Jacob “died in faith, not having received the promises” (Heb 11:9, 13), being made perfect only together with the faithful of later times (Heb 11:39–40). From the verses: the promise of Canaan was made to Abraham in person and has not yet been kept to him; it awaits his resurrection, when he and his seed, which is Christ (Gal 3:16), inherit the land for ever.

note: Drafted 2026-11-19. Root key כנע (BDB k.cd.aa). Keys assigned: k.cd.aa verb, k.cd.ab כִּנְעָה, k.cd.ac כְּנַעַן, k.cd.ae כְּנַעֲנִי; k.cd.ag is the name Kenaanah in names/kenaanah.json. k.cd.ad (כְּנַעַן “merchant”) and k.cd.af (כְּנַעֲנִי “trader”) list exactly the same occurrences as k.cd.ac and k.cd.ae, so, as the README says, only one key is named for each; their sense is a sense of the name and the gentilic (ids merchants, trader). Isa 23:8 כִּנְעָנֶיהָ is filed by the corpus under כְּנַעַן but is the plural of כְּנַעֲנִי. Canaan and Canaanite are kept in this entry: they are spelled with the root, nothing puts them under another root, and scripture twice uses the verb of subduing Canaan (Jdg 4:23; Neh 9:24); but no verse explains the name, so the tie to “be brought low” rests on little. Canaan son of Ham is a TIPNR person (Canaan@Gen.9.18) but has no name file: the name is the land's and people's as much as the man's (as Mizraim in mitsrayim). Leads not followed: Arabic كنع (Lane p. 2634 says “See Supplement”, not vendored; Klein's “be contracted, wrinkled, fold the wings”, a possible cognate of the verb and of כִּנְעָה “pack”); Arabic qanaʿa “be content” and Ge'ez ʾaqnəʿa are q, not k, and not regular; Akkadian kanāšu “bow down, submit” is kns/knš, not this root; Ugaritic knʿny “Canaanite” (DULAT, not vendored) would show ʿ directly; Phoenician in Krahmalkov not checked by page; Arabic كنعان is the name as known from scripture and is not recorded. The Peshitta's קנָנָיָא (Mat 10:4, Simon “the Cananaean”) is of the root קנא “zeal”, not this one. Greek: ἐντρέπω renders the niphal at Lev 26:41; 2Ki 22:19; 2Ch 12:7; 30:11; 36:12 (“be put to shame, turn in respect”), not recorded. Open questions: (1) whether the name Canaan belongs to כנע “be low” at all; (2) whether כִּנְעָה is “pack” from “press together” or “wares” from כְּנַעַן “merchant”; (3) the doctrine statements are reasoned conclusions to review.
